questions.question: At what point does partitioning become necessary?

options.text: When the data or query load outgrows a single machine
As soon as more than one machine is available to the system
Whenever a secondary index has to be maintained
Only once replication has been exhausted as an option

questions.explanation: Partitioning, also called sharding, is for very large datasets or very high query throughput — the goal being to spread data and query load evenly across machines.

questions.question: In a distributed database, under what conditions is replication alone not enough, and what other name is used for partitioning?

options.text: Very large datasets or very high query throughput; partitioning is also called sharding
Read-heavy workloads with many more reads than writes; partitioning is also called striping
Clusters where nodes fail frequently; partitioning is also called federation
Users spread across many regions; partitioning is also called edge caching

questions.explanation: Replication keeps a full copy of the same data on several nodes, so every replica must still hold the whole dataset and apply every write. That helps with read scaling, fault tolerance and serving distant users, but it does not help when the data is too big for one machine or the write load too high for one node. Partitioning, also called sharding, splits the data so each node holds and serves only a subset.

questions.question: In distributed data systems, the word 'partition' names two unrelated things. Which two?

options.text: Deliberately splitting a database, versus a network fault between nodes
Disk partitions on one machine, versus database partitions across machines
Horizontal partitioning of rows, versus vertical partitioning of columns
Logical partition boundaries, versus the physical files that hold them

questions.explanation: A database partition (shard) is a deliberate design choice: a large dataset is split into smaller subsets placed on different nodes. A network partition (netsplit) is a fault in which the network between nodes fails, so some nodes cannot reach others. The two share a word but nothing else; horizontal versus vertical splitting and logical versus physical layout are both aspects of the first meaning, not a second meaning.

questions.question: Different systems use different words for a partition. Which pairings are right? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: shard in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and SolrCloud
region in HBase, and tablet in Bigtable
vnode in Cassandra and Riak, and vBucket in Couchbase
chunk in Kafka and segment in Voldemort

questions.explanation: Shard, region, tablet, vnode and vBucket are product-specific names for a partition. Kafka commonly calls its unit a partition, so the chunk/segment pairing is incorrect.

optionExplanations.a: MongoDB, Elasticsearch and SolrCloud use shard for a logical data subdivision, even though their placement and replication details differ.
optionExplanations.b: HBase calls a key-range partition a region, while Bigtable calls the corresponding range unit a tablet.
optionExplanations.c: Cassandra and Riak use vnode for virtual partitions, and Couchbase calls its comparable routing unit a vBucket.
optionExplanations.d: Kafka itself uses the term partition, and Voldemort uses partition-related terminology rather than the claimed chunk/segment pairing.

questions.question: In a partitioned database, how many partitions does each record normally belong to?

options.text: Exactly one partition, although replication may store copies of it on several nodes
Several partitions, so that losing one partition does not lose the record
One partition per replica, so a record with three replicas belongs to three partitions
One partition per secondary index, since each index is partitioned separately

questions.explanation: Partitions are normally defined so each record, row or document belongs to exactly one partition; in effect each partition is a small database of its own. Redundancy comes from replication, which copies the whole partition to several nodes, not from putting the record in several partitions. Secondary indexes may be partitioned differently, but the record itself still has one owning partition.

questions.question: What is the main reason to partition data, and what does partitioning let a shared-nothing cluster spread out?

options.text: Scalability: the dataset is spread over many disks and the query load over many processors
Availability: copies of every record are spread over many nodes so one failure loses nothing
Latency: data is spread over regions so each user is served from a nearby copy
Durability: each acknowledged write is spread over several disks before it is confirmed

questions.explanation: Partitioning exists for scalability. In a shared-nothing cluster each partition can live on a different node, so storage is spread across many disks and query work across many processors; single-partition queries can then run independently on each node. Availability, low latency for distant users and durability come mainly from replication (keeping copies), not from splitting the data.

questions.question: In a partitioned database, how does partitioning affect the scalability of queries?

options.text: Single-partition queries scale by adding nodes; large queries can be parallelized, but that is much harder
Every query scales linearly with node count, including joins and aggregations across partitions
Only single-partition queries benefit; complex queries can never be parallelized across nodes
Complex queries scale better than simple ones, because they touch more nodes at once

questions.explanation: Independent single-partition requests scale naturally because each node serves its own subset. Large analytical queries can parallelize scans and stages, but coordinating joins, aggregation, and result exchange is substantially harder.

questions.question: Which systems pioneered partitioned databases?

options.text: Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL, in the 1980s
Oracle and DB2, in the 1990s
Google Bigtable and Amazon Dynamo, in the 2000s
IBM IMS, in the 1970s

questions.explanation: Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL pioneered partitioned databases in the 1980s. Bigtable, Dynamo and other NoSQL systems and Hadoop-based warehouses came later and rediscovered the idea rather than inventing it; IMS was a hierarchical single-machine database.

questions.question: Some partitioned systems target transactional workloads and others analytics. What does that difference affect, and what does it not?

options.text: It changes how the system is tuned, not the fundamentals of partitioning
It changes the partitioning algorithm itself, which differs entirely between the two
It changes nothing at all, since partitioning is invisible to the workload
It changes the replication scheme, though the tuning stays the same

questions.explanation: Transactional systems optimize many small, low-latency requests, while analytical systems optimize large scans and parallel stages. Both still face the same core placement, skew and rebalancing problems.

questions.question: A colleague reads that each record belongs to exactly one partition and concludes it lives on exactly one machine. Correct them.

options.text: It belongs to one partition, but copies of that partition may sit on several nodes
They are correct: one partition always means exactly one machine
Each record is stored on every machine in the cluster at once
A record is split by column across several partitions on different machines

questions.explanation: Belonging to a partition is a logical assignment; where that partition is stored is physical. Partitioning is usually combined with replication, so copies of each partition sit on several nodes for fault tolerance. The record still has one owning partition, but it may be stored on several machines.

questions.question: When partitioning is combined with leader–follower replication, how are leaders and followers placed?

options.text: Each node leads some partitions and follows others
One node is leader for all partitions and the rest are followers
Each node is either a pure leader node or a pure follower node for all its partitions
Every node acts as leader for every partition

questions.explanation: A balanced replicated cluster spreads leadership rather than assigning one global leader. Each node leads some partitions and stores follower copies of others, distributing writes and failover capacity.

questions.question: In a partitioned and replicated database, how are the choice of partitioning scheme and the choice of replication scheme related?

options.text: They are mostly independent design choices
Partitioning fully determines the replication scheme, so both must be chosen together
Replication must be disabled when partitioning is used
Replication makes partitioning unnecessary, since every node already holds the data

questions.explanation: Partitioning decides which logical subset owns a record; replication decides how many copies of that subset exist and how they stay consistent. They can usually be chosen separately, although placement and failover policies must coordinate both.

questions.question: If data and query load are spread perfectly evenly, how should 10 nodes compare with a single node (ignoring replication)?

options.text: Ten nodes should handle ten times the data and throughput
Ten nodes should handle roughly twice the data of a single node
Ten nodes should handle ten times the data but the same throughput
Throughput scales with nodes while total data volume does not

questions.explanation: Ignoring replication overhead, ideal horizontal scaling is linear: ten comparable nodes hold about ten times the data and serve about ten times the throughput of one.

questions.question: What are skew and a hot spot in a partitioned system?

options.text: Skew is uneven load; a hot spot is an overloaded partition
Skew means clock drift between nodes; a hot spot is an overheated machine
Skew means variance in network latency; a hot spot is a cache miss storm
Skew means having too many partitions; a hot spot means having too few

questions.explanation: Skew means data or requests are distributed unevenly, and the disproportionately busy partition is a hot spot. In the extreme, one partition serves all traffic while nine of ten nodes sit idle, defeating horizontal scaling.

questions.question: Assigning each record to a randomly chosen node would avoid hot spots. What does that get right, and what is the big disadvantage?

options.text: Even data spread, but a read must query all nodes, as the key's node is unknown
Data spreads evenly, but every write must be sent to every node to keep copies in sync
Reads become fast, but data clusters on a few nodes because random choices repeat
Point lookups stay fast, but range queries become impossible

questions.explanation: Random placement balances data, but it provides no deterministic route from a key to its node. Every lookup would become a scatter/gather request, trading balanced writes for expensive reads.

questions.question: With key-range partitioning, what must a client know to send a request for a key directly to the right node?

options.text: The range boundaries between partitions and which node each partition is assigned to
Only the hash function, since key-range partitions are located by hashing the key
Only the number of nodes, since the key space is always split into equal ranges
Only the partition-to-node map, since every range covers the same number of keys

questions.explanation: Key-range partitioning assigns each partition a continuous interval of keys. A client can route directly only if it knows both the interval boundaries and which node currently owns each interval.

questions.question: In a print encyclopedia partitioned by key range, volume 1 covers A and B while volume 12 covers T, U, V, X, Y and Z. What design conclusion follows?

options.text: Partition boundaries should adapt to the data, because keys are not evenly distributed
Each partition should cover the same number of letters, so volumes stay equal
Range partitioning cannot handle uneven data, so hash partitioning is required
Boundaries are fixed once chosen, so the uneven split must be accepted

questions.explanation: Words are not evenly spread across the alphabet, so one volume per two letters would make some volumes far bigger than others. To spread data evenly, key-range boundaries must follow the actual distribution; they can be chosen by an administrator or automatically by the database, and can be adjusted later.

questions.question: Which statements about key-range partitioning are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Its boundaries can be chosen manually by an administrator or automatically by the database
Bigtable and its open source equivalent HBase use it
RethinkDB uses it, as did MongoDB before version 2.4
Cassandra and Riak use it to place their primary data

questions.explanation: Key-range partitioning gives each partition a contiguous range of keys; its boundaries may be set by an administrator or chosen automatically. Bigtable, HBase and RethinkDB use it, and MongoDB used only range-based sharding until version 2.4 added hash-based sharding. Cassandra and Riak place data by a hash of the key.

optionExplanations.a: Boundaries can be configured by hand when the key distribution is known, or chosen and adjusted automatically by the database as partitions grow.
optionExplanations.b: Bigtable tablets and HBase regions each own a contiguous, sorted range of keys, which makes range scans within a partition efficient.
optionExplanations.c: RethinkDB partitions by key range, and MongoDB offered only range-based sharding until hash-based sharding arrived in version 2.4.
optionExplanations.d: Cassandra and Riak hash keys to choose a partition; Cassandra sorts by the later columns of a compound key only within a partition, which is not global key-range placement.

questions.question: What does keeping keys sorted within each partition buy?

options.text: Easy range scans, and use of the key as a concatenated index
Point lookups become constant time rather than logarithmic
Cross-partition joins become possible without extra coordination
Writes become sequential, removing the need for compaction

questions.explanation: Because keys remain ordered within a partition, the storage engine can scan a contiguous interval efficiently. Compound keys can use this ordering as an index over related records such as one user's timestamped events.

questions.question: If sensor measurements are key-range partitioned by an increasing timestamp, what hot-spot failure occurs?

options.text: A timestamp key sends all of today's writes to one partition
Reads scatter across all partitions, making range queries slow
Partitions grow without bound and cannot be split
Timestamps cannot be used as keys at all

questions.explanation: All current timestamps fall at the high end of the key space, so today's writes concentrate on the one partition owning that range. Older partitions receive little or no write traffic.

questions.question: Sensor readings keyed by timestamp under key-range partitioning send all current writes to one partition. How can the key be changed to spread the writes?

options.text: Prefix each timestamp with the sensor name, so keys sort by sensor, then time
Hash the timestamp, keeping efficient time-range scans across all sensors
Create a new partition for each hour of readings instead of one per day
Suffix each timestamp with the sensor name, so keys still sort by time first

questions.explanation: A sensor-ID prefix sends different sensors' current writes to different key ranges. The trade-off is that a time-range query across all sensors must query and combine many sensor-specific ranges.

questions.question: A partitioning hash function maps a string key to a 32-bit value. What is its output range and key property?

options.text: A number from 0 to 2 to the 32nd minus 1, evenly spread even for very similar inputs
A number from 0 to 2 to the 16th, with similar inputs producing similar hashes
A number from 0 to 2 to the 32nd minus 1, with similar inputs landing close together to keep locality
A 256-bit cryptographic digest that cannot be reversed

questions.explanation: A 32-bit hash produces values from 0 through 2 to the 32nd minus 1. For partitioning, the key property is that even very similar input strings get hashes spread evenly over that whole range, which turns skewed keys into a uniform distribution. A hash that kept similar inputs close together would preserve exactly the clustering that causes hot spots, and cryptographic strength is not needed.

questions.question: What properties should a database partitioning hash have?

options.text: Stable, repeatable output with a uniform distribution
It must be cryptographically strong, so SHA-256 is effectively required
Any built-in hash will do, including Java's Object.hashCode() method
It must be reversible, so that the original key can be recovered

questions.explanation: A partition hash needs repeatable, well-distributed output rather than cryptographic strength. Language runtimes may randomize built-in hashes between processes, so systems use stable algorithms such as MD5 or FNV instead.

questions.question: How does hash partitioning assign keys to partitions?

options.text: Each partition owns a range of hash values; a key goes where its hash falls
Each partition owns a range of keys, and the hash is used only to check data integrity
Each key goes to a randomly chosen partition, recorded in a lookup table
Each partition owns a fixed list of keys, recomputed on every write to the store

questions.explanation: Hashing converts arbitrary keys into a bounded numeric space, and each partition owns a range in that space. The range boundaries may be evenly spaced or chosen pseudorandomly.

questions.question: What is consistent hashing as originally defined?

options.text: Karger et al.'s scheme for spreading load across internet-wide caches
A database rebalancing algorithm defined by Amazon for the Dynamo paper
A hash function whose output stays stable across separate processes
A method for maintaining key order within a single partition

questions.explanation: Karger-style consistent hashing assigns cache objects around a hash ring so membership changes move relatively few objects. It was designed for decentralized internet caches, not as a general name for database hash partitioning.

questions.question: For what kind of system was consistent hashing, as defined by Karger et al., designed?

options.text: Spreading load across an internet-wide system of caches, such as a CDN
Rebalancing partitions inside a database cluster, where it is the standard method
Keeping replicas consistent with each other after a leader failover
Enforcing ACID consistency for transactions that span several partitions

questions.explanation: Karger et al. designed consistent hashing to spread load across internet-wide cache systems such as CDNs, using randomly chosen partition boundaries so no central control or consensus is needed. The word 'consistent' has nothing to do with replica consistency or ACID consistency. The approach does not work very well for databases and is rarely used as originally defined, and database documentation often uses the name loosely, so 'hash partitioning' is the clearer term.

questions.question: What important capability does hash partitioning sacrifice?

options.text: Efficient range queries over the primary key, because adjacent keys are scattered
Efficient point lookups by primary key, because every partition must be searched
The ability to rebalance, because hash ranges can never be reassigned
Even data distribution, because similar keys collide on the same partition

questions.explanation: Hashing spreads adjacent source keys across unrelated hash values, so a range query must scatter rather than scan one ordered interval. MongoDB hash sharding does this; Riak, Couchbase and Voldemort omit primary-key range queries.

questions.question: How does Cassandra partition and order a compound primary key?

options.text: Hash the first component; sort by the rest
Hash the entire compound key and discard component ordering
Keep the first component ordered and use the rest only for routing
Hash the final component and use earlier components as clustering keys

questions.explanation: The first component keeps one entity's related rows together, while the remaining columns provide an ordered index inside that partition. It cannot efficiently range-scan across different first-component values.

questions.question: Cassandra can hash the first column of a compound primary key to pick the partition and sort rows by the remaining columns. Which data shape suits this best?

options.text: One-to-many data, such as all updates by one user ordered by timestamp
Many-to-many relationships traversed in both directions
Aggregations that scan every user's data at once
Range queries over the first key column, such as all user IDs between 1000 and 2000

questions.explanation: With a key such as (user_id, update_timestamp), the hashed user_id keeps one user's rows together on one partition while different users spread across partitions, and the timestamp orders that user's updates. That makes 'all updates by this user in a time interval' an efficient range scan. A range over the first column itself is not efficient, because hashing scatters different user IDs.

questions.question: Hashing reduces hot spots but can't avoid them entirely. What is the extreme case, and why is hashing powerless?

options.text: All requests target one key, and an identical key always hashes the same
There are too many distinct keys, and hashing makes them collide
The database is empty, so hashing has nothing yet to distribute across partitions
Keys arrive in sequence, and hashing preserves their order on the partitions

questions.explanation: A deterministic hash must send every occurrence of the same key to the same partition. If one key receives nearly all traffic, no uniform distribution across different keys can split that single-key load.

questions.question: With hash partitioning, how can an application spread the writes for one known-hot key, such as a celebrity's user ID?

options.text: Append a random number to the key, so writes spread over many keys that reads must combine
Hash the key with a stronger hash function so its writes spread over several partitions
Add more replicas of the key's partition so its writes spread across the replicas
Move the key to a dedicated, more powerful node so no other partition is affected

questions.explanation: Appending a two-digit random number turns one logical key into 100 physical keys, which hash to different partitions, so writes spread out. The cost is on reads: they must fetch all 100 keys and combine them. A different hash function cannot help, because one identical key always gets one hash, and extra replicas do not split writes, since every replica must apply every write.

questions.question: Besides querying every suffix, which bookkeeping costs does random-suffix splitting of a hot key introduce? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The extra overhead means it should be applied only to the few hot keys, not to every key
You need some way of keeping track of which keys are being split
It requires the hash function to be cryptographically strong, or the split is uneven
It requires replication to be disabled while the split key is in use

questions.explanation: Random-suffix splitting adds overhead, so it only makes sense for the small number of keys with very high write throughput; for most keys it would be pure cost. Because only some keys are split, the system or application must also record which keys are split so readers know to fetch and combine every suffix. Neither cryptographic hashing nor disabling replication is involved.

optionExplanations.a: Every split logical key multiplies storage and read fan-out, so applying suffixes to ordinary cold keys would add cost without relieving meaningful load.
optionExplanations.b: Readers and writers need metadata identifying which logical keys use suffixes and how many suffixes exist, otherwise they cannot find every fragment.
optionExplanations.c: A stable, well-distributed noncryptographic hash or random suffix is sufficient; cryptographic strength is unrelated to whether the hot-key fragments spread.
optionExplanations.d: Replication can continue for each suffixed physical key and need not be disabled; hot-key splitting changes key layout rather than replica semantics.

questions.question: In most data systems as of the mid-2010s, who has to reduce the skew caused by a single, known-hot key?

options.text: The application, usually by changing how that key is written
The database, which detects and splits hot keys automatically
The network layer, which spreads requests for the key across nodes
Nobody, because single-key skew cannot be reduced at all

questions.explanation: As of the mid-2010s most data systems could not automatically compensate for a highly skewed workload on one key, so it was the application's job, for example by adding random suffixes to the hot key. Hashing alone does not help because identical keys hash identically. Automatic detection of hot keys was a hoped-for future capability rather than a standard feature.

questions.question: In a partitioned database, what are the two main ways to partition a secondary index?

options.text: By document (a local index in each partition) or by term (a global index)
Eagerly on every write, or lazily the next time the index is read
With write-through caching of the index, or with write-back caching
Through synchronous index replication, or through asynchronous replication

questions.explanation: A secondary index searches by a value other than the primary key, such as color:red, so it does not map neatly onto primary-key partitions. Document-based partitioning keeps a local index in each partition covering only its own documents; term-based partitioning builds a global index that is itself partitioned by the indexed value. Eager versus lazy updating, caching policy and replication mode describe update timing or copying, not where index entries are placed.

questions.question: How does secondary-index support vary across systems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Secondary indexes are the bread and butter of relational databases, and they are common in document databases too
Many key-value stores such as HBase and Voldemort have avoided secondary indexes because of their added implementation complexity
No key-value store can offer secondary indexes, because the key-value model cannot express them
Secondary indexes are the raison d'être of search servers such as Solr and Elasticsearch

questions.explanation: Relational and document databases commonly support secondary indexes, and search servers exist mainly to provide them. Some key-value stores avoided them because they are complex to implement in a distributed system, but the model does not forbid them: Riak, a key-value store, added secondary indexes because they are so useful for data modeling.

optionExplanations.a: Relational query planning relies heavily on non-primary indexes, and document stores commonly index fields other than the document ID.
optionExplanations.b: Distributed secondary indexes need extra writes and cross-partition coordination, so stores such as HBase and Voldemort left them out and pushed the work to applications.
optionExplanations.c: Avoiding secondary indexes is an implementation choice, not a limit of the model; Riak is a key-value store that added secondary indexes.
optionExplanations.d: Solr and Elasticsearch are search servers whose central purpose is building indexes over document terms and fields.

questions.question: A used-car site is partitioned by document ID (IDs 0 to 499 in partition 0, 500 to 999 in partition 1) and uses document-partitioned secondary indexes. A red car with ID 742 is added. Which color:red index entry is updated?

options.text: Only the one in partition 1's local index, because the car's document lives in partition 1
The entries in both partitions' indexes, because red cars exist in each
Only the one in partition 0, because colors starting with a to r are stored there
One on a separate global index node that holds all color entries

questions.explanation: With document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes, each partition indexes only the documents it stores. ID 742 falls in the 500 to 999 range, so the document lives in partition 1, and only partition 1 adds 742 to its own color:red list. Partition 0 may also have red cars in its own list, but it is not touched by this write. Placing entries by the color term would describe a term-partitioned (global) index instead.

questions.question: If your database supports only a key-value model and you build a secondary index yourself in application code (a mapping from values to document IDs), which hazards should you watch for? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Race conditions between concurrent writers updating the record and the index
Partial write failures that save the record but not the index entry, or the reverse
Hash collisions between two different secondary index values
Physical fragmentation of the index file as documents are updated

questions.explanation: An application-maintained index updates both the source record and a value-to-ID mapping. Concurrent writers or a partial failure between those writes can make them disagree, so atomic multi-object updates or careful repair are needed.

optionExplanations.a: Concurrent updates can interleave changes to the source record and application-maintained index, leaving an entry missing, duplicated or pointing at stale data.
optionExplanations.b: If one of the two writes fails after the other succeeds, the index and underlying record diverge unless a transaction or repair process reconciles them.
optionExplanations.c: Hash collisions are handled by normal key equality and bucket logic; they are not the central consistency hazard of maintaining a secondary index in application code.
optionExplanations.d: Physical file fragmentation is an engine-level storage concern and does not explain why a value-to-record mapping becomes logically inconsistent.

questions.question: With document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes, what does a write that adds, removes or updates a document have to update?

options.text: Only the partition holding that document, including that partition's own secondary indexes
The secondary index on every partition, since any partition may be queried
A central index server that holds the secondary index for all partitions
Nothing immediately; the secondary indexes are rebuilt by a periodic batch job

questions.explanation: Each partition indexes only its own documents, so a write updates the record and local index on one partition. That cheap write path is the main benefit; reads may need scatter/gather.

questions.question: How is a query on a document-partitioned (local) secondary index, such as 'find all red cars', executed?

options.text: Send it to every partition and merge the results (scatter/gather)
Query the partitions one after another and stop at the first match
Send it only to the partition chosen by hashing the search term
Run it inside a distributed transaction across all partitions

questions.explanation: A local secondary index contains matches only from its own data partition. The coordinator must query every partition and wait for the slowest relevant response, so scatter/gather amplifies tail latency.

questions.question: Which statements about document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud and VoltDB all use them
Most vendors recommend choosing the partitioning so that secondary-index queries can be served from a single partition
Serving every secondary-index query from one partition is not always possible, especially when a query filters on several indexes such as car color and make
Vendors recommend always using term-partitioned indexes instead, since reads dominate

questions.explanation: Document-partitioned indexes keep writes local and are therefore common, but a query may need every partition. Choosing a partition key that serves common index queries locally avoids scatter/gather when the access pattern permits it.

optionExplanations.a: The listed systems keep secondary-index entries in each document's own partition, so a document write updates only local index structures.
optionExplanations.b: If common queries include the partition key, the router can target one local index and avoid the latency and load of scatter/gather.
optionExplanations.c: Queries combining independent attributes such as color and make may match records on many partitions, so no single partitioning choice keeps every such query local.
optionExplanations.d: Term-partitioned indexes trade cheaper reads for cross-partition write complexity; vendors do not recommend them universally just because some workloads read often.

questions.question: In term-partitioned (global) secondary indexing, why must the global index itself be partitioned rather than stored on one node?

options.text: Because one node holding the whole index would become a bottleneck
Because a secondary index is always larger than the data it indexes
Because no single node is ever able to hold an entire index
Because each index entry must live in the same partition as its document

questions.explanation: A global index covers data from all partitions. Putting it on one node would funnel every index read and write through that node, recreating the bottleneck partitioning was meant to remove. So the global index is partitioned too, but by the indexed term rather than by primary key. Storing entries with their documents would make it a local index, not a global one.

questions.question: A term-partitioned secondary index on car color puts colors starting a to r in index partition 0 and s to z in index partition 1. A red car is stored in data partition 1. Where is its color:red index entry written?

options.text: In index partition 0, because the term color:red falls in the a to r range
In index partition 1, because the car's document lives in data partition 1
In both index partitions, because each one indexes every color
In whichever index partition is least loaded at write time

questions.explanation: In a term-partitioned (global) index, the indexed term decides the index partition, independently of where the document is stored. 'red' starts with r, inside the a to r range, so the entry goes to index partition 0 even though the car itself is in data partition 1. That is why one document write can touch index partitions on other nodes, and why all red cars can be found by reading a single index partition.

questions.question: In a term-partitioned (global) secondary index, what determines which partition holds an index entry?

options.text: The indexed term (such as color:red) or its hash
The document ID of the record that is being indexed
The node that happened to receive the write
The time at which the index entry was first written

questions.explanation: The indexed value chooses the partition, so all entries for color:red can reside together. The word 'term' comes from full-text search, where each indexed word is a search term.

questions.question: In a term-partitioned secondary index, what is the trade-off of partitioning by a hash of the term rather than by the term itself?

options.text: More even load, but no efficient range scans over terms such as price
Range scans over terms become possible, but load concentrates on a few partitions
Hashing changes nothing, because indexed terms are already evenly distributed
Term order is kept, so both range scans and even load are preserved

questions.explanation: Partitioning by the term itself keeps terms in sorted order, so a range scan, such as cars with an asking price in some band, reads a contiguous range. Hashing the term scatters nearby terms across partitions, which spreads load more evenly but makes such range scans inefficient. This is the same order-versus-evenness trade-off as key-range versus hash partitioning of primary keys.

questions.question: Compared with a document-partitioned (local) index, how does a term-partitioned (global) index shift query cost?

options.text: Reads can go to one index partition, but a write may update several index partitions
Reads still need scatter/gather, but a write touches only one index partition
Reads and writes both get cheaper, since each touches only one partition
Costs stay the same for reads and writes; only the index's total size differs

questions.explanation: A term points directly to one global index partition, avoiding read scatter/gather. Updating a document may affect several term partitions, moving coordination and latency onto the write path.

questions.question: In a term-partitioned (global) secondary index, what would it take for every document write to be reflected in the index immediately?

options.text: A distributed transaction across every affected partition
Only a local transaction on the partition being written to
A nightly batch job that rebuilds the whole index from scratch
Independent local transactions on the data and index partitions

questions.explanation: Keeping a global term index immediately current may require one atomic transaction across the data partition and every affected index partition. Systems commonly avoid that coordination by updating the index asynchronously.

questions.question: In practice, how are global (term-partitioned) secondary indexes usually updated?

options.text: Asynchronously, so a read shortly after a write may not yet see the change
Synchronously in a distributed transaction, so the index is never stale
By a nightly batch job that rebuilds the whole index
Lazily on read, by scanning every data partition when the index is queried

questions.explanation: Keeping a global index exactly current would need a distributed transaction across every partition a write affects, which not all databases support. So updates are usually asynchronous: the index catches up shortly after the write, and a read in between may miss the change. Amazon DynamoDB, for example, documented around 2014 that its global secondary indexes update within a fraction of a second normally but can lag longer during infrastructure faults.

questions.question: Which changes over time call for rebalancing partitions across the nodes of a database cluster? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The query throughput increases, so you want to add more CPUs to handle the load
The dataset size increases, so you want to add more disks and RAM to store it
A machine fails, and other machines need to take over the failed machine's responsibilities
The document schema changes, which forces the whole index to be rebuilt

questions.explanation: Rebalancing is moving data and requests from one node to another. It is needed when cluster capacity or membership changes: more query throughput calls for more CPUs, a bigger dataset for more disks and RAM, and a failed machine's partitions must be taken over by others. A schema change alters what is stored, not which node owns which partition.

optionExplanations.a: Rising request throughput can exhaust the processors serving current partitions, motivating new nodes and redistribution of request load.
optionExplanations.b: Dataset growth can exceed existing disk or memory capacity, so adding storage-bearing nodes requires partitions to move.
optionExplanations.c: After a machine fails, surviving nodes must assume its partition responsibilities to restore balanced service and replication.
optionExplanations.d: A schema change may require index maintenance, but it does not inherently change node capacity or require cluster-wide partition ownership to be rebalanced.

questions.question: What are the minimum requirements rebalancing is expected to meet? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: After rebalancing, the load — data storage, read and write requests — should be shared fairly between the nodes in the cluster
While rebalancing is happening, the database should continue accepting reads and writes
No more data than necessary should be moved between nodes, to make rebalancing fast and to minimize the network and disk I/O load
Rebalancing should always complete within a fixed, configurable time bound

questions.explanation: Good rebalancing restores fair storage and request load, keeps reads and writes available during movement, and transfers only necessary data. A universal fixed completion time is unrealistic under variable data and network load.

optionExplanations.a: The goal is to remove overloaded and underused nodes by redistributing both stored bytes and request traffic according to available capacity.
optionExplanations.b: Taking the database offline would turn routine growth or membership changes into outages, so production rebalancing should preserve read and write service.
optionExplanations.c: Partition transfers consume disk and network resources; minimizing moved data shortens the operation and reduces interference with foreground work.
optionExplanations.d: Completion time depends on partition sizes, workload, bandwidth and failures, so no fixed bound can be guaranteed for every rebalance.

questions.question: Under hash mod N placement (node number = hash(key) mod N), a key hashes to 123456. Which node holds it with 10, 11, 12 and 13 nodes?

options.text: Nodes 6, 3, 0 and 8, so the key moves almost every time N changes
Node 6 in all four cases, because the key's hash value stays fixed
Nodes 6, 7, 8 and 9, because adding a node shifts the key by one
Nodes 6, 6, 0 and 0, because only every second change of N moves the key

questions.explanation: 123456 mod 10 = 6; mod 11 = 3 (11 × 11223 = 123453); mod 12 = 0 (12 × 10288 = 123456); mod 13 = 8 (13 × 9496 = 123448). The hash is fixed, but the remainder depends on N, so changing the node count moves most keys to a different node. That makes rebalancing very expensive, which is why systems instead assign ranges of hashes to partitions and move whole partitions.

questions.question: A 10-node cluster was set up with 1,000 partitions, about 100 per node. Under fixed-partition rebalancing, what happens when an 11th node joins?

options.text: The new node takes a few whole partitions from each existing node, about 91 in total
The partition count grows to 1,100 and all keys are rehashed
The new node creates 100 new, empty partitions and the others keep theirs
Some existing partitions are split in half and the new node takes one half of each

questions.explanation: Fixed partitioning creates many more partitions than nodes up front and only changes which node owns each whole partition. With 1,000 partitions over 11 nodes, each node should own about 91, so the newcomer takes roughly 9 from each existing node. The number of partitions and the key-to-partition mapping stay the same; splitting partitions for a new node is a different scheme (partitions proportional to nodes).

questions.question: In fixed-partition rebalancing, what changes when partitions move and what stays the same?

options.text: Only which node owns each whole partition changes; the key-to-partition mapping stays fixed
Keys are reassigned to different partitions, and the partition count grows
The number of partitions changes, but each key stays on the same node
The partition count stays fixed, but keys shift to neighbouring partitions to balance sizes

questions.explanation: The hash or range rule keeps mapping each key to the same logical partition, and the number of partitions does not change. Rebalancing only changes which node owns each whole partition. Because moving a partition takes time, the old assignment keeps serving reads and writes while the transfer is in progress.

questions.question: Your cluster has some much more powerful machines. What does the fixed-partition scheme let you do?

options.text: Give more partitions to the more powerful nodes
Keep partition counts equal, since every node must hold the same number
Give the powerful nodes larger partitions
Disable rebalancing on the weaker nodes

questions.explanation: Because partitions are independent placement units, a stronger machine can own more of them than a weaker machine. Partition counts thereby approximate each node's storage and throughput capacity.

questions.question: With a fixed number of partitions that is set when the database is created and never split, what limits how far the cluster can grow?

options.text: The partition count caps the node count, so set it high enough for growth
There is no limit, because new nodes trigger partition splits automatically
The cluster can never grow beyond the number of nodes it started with
Each partition has a configured maximum size, which caps the total data volume

questions.explanation: Each node needs at least one partition, so the fixed count caps the node count unless splitting is added. Riak, Elasticsearch, Couchbase and Voldemort use this model. Too few partitions become large and costly to move; too many add overhead.

questions.question: How do key-range-partitioned databases such as HBase and RethinkDB keep partitions balanced as data grows unevenly?

options.text: Split large ranges and merge small adjacent ranges
They use hash partitioning instead, avoiding the problem
They require the administrator to preconfigure exact boundaries
They never split partitions, relying on large nodes

questions.explanation: Fixed key boundaries can leave one range holding most of the data. Dynamic range partitioning behaves like a B-tree: oversized ranges split, while small neighboring ranges merge.

questions.question: In dynamic key-range partitioning (for example, HBase), what can happen after a large partition splits in two?

options.text: One of the two halves can be transferred to another node to balance load
Both halves must stay on the original node, since a node owns one contiguous range
Both halves must move to new nodes, freeing the original node
The halves are merged back as soon as the write burst passes

questions.explanation: The two halves remain separate logical partitions, and the system may move one half to balance load. Each partition has one owner while a node may own many; the partition count grows with data volume.

questions.question: With dynamic key-range partitioning, an empty database starts with a single partition, so all early writes hit one node. How do HBase and MongoDB mitigate this?

options.text: Pre-splitting: configure initial partitions using the expected key distribution
Setting the split threshold to zero so every write creates a new partition
Letting each node create its own first partition, so no mitigation is needed
Hashing all keys until the first split, then switching back to key ranges

questions.explanation: An empty database may begin with one partition, concentrating all early writes on one node. Pre-splitting distributes those writes immediately, but requires advance knowledge of the likely key distribution.

questions.question: True or false: dynamic partitioning applies only to key range–partitioned data.

options.text: False — it works with hash partitioning too, as MongoDB shows
True — hash partitioning always uses a fixed number of partitions
True — only HBase and RethinkDB support it, and both are key-range
False — it applies only to hash-partitioned data

questions.explanation: Dynamic partitioning means partitions can split as they grow; it does not require source-key ranges. MongoDB can split ranges of hash values just as another system splits ranges of original keys.

questions.question: Three partitioning schemes differ in what is proportional to what. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: With dynamic partitioning, the number of partitions is proportional to dataset size
With a fixed number of partitions, the size of each partition is proportional to dataset size
With either dynamic partitioning or a fixed partition count, the number of partitions grows in step with the number of nodes
With a fixed number of partitions per node, partition count is proportional to node count

questions.explanation: Dynamic partitioning keeps partition size within bounds, so partition count grows with data. A fixed-count design instead lets each partition grow with the dataset. Cassandra/Ketama-style designs keep partitions per node roughly fixed, so total partition count grows with node count.

optionExplanations.a: Dynamic schemes split oversized partitions and may merge small ones, so more data generally creates more partitions while keeping each within target bounds.
optionExplanations.b: When the total partition count cannot change, dataset growth is absorbed by larger average partitions rather than by creating new ones.
optionExplanations.c: Dynamic partitions track data volume and fixed partitions do not grow with node count, so neither of those schemes necessarily ties partition count to nodes.
optionExplanations.d: Keeping a fixed number of virtual partitions per node makes the cluster's total partition count increase as nodes are added.

questions.question: In partitioning proportional to nodes (a fixed number of partitions per node, as in Cassandra), what happens when a new node joins?

options.text: Split selected partitions and give it one half of each
The new node takes whole partitions from existing nodes, with no splitting
All partitions are recomputed from scratch, doubling the count
The new node creates 256 empty partitions and waits for writes

questions.explanation: The new node chooses a fixed number of existing partitions, splits them, and takes one half of each. Cassandra historically used about 256 partitions per node so many random shares average toward fair load.

questions.question: When a joining node picks partition boundaries at random (as in partitioning proportional to nodes), why must hash-based partitioning be used?

options.text: Because boundaries can be drawn from the hash's numeric range
Because hashing is what makes the keys sortable in the first place
Because raw keys cannot be compared to one another at all
It does not require hashing; raw keys work equally well for sampling

questions.explanation: A hash function maps arbitrary keys into a known numeric space, so a joining node can select boundary positions without knowing the original key distribution. Raw ordered keys generally do not offer that uniform numeric space.

questions.question: What lies between fully automatic and fully manual rebalancing of partitions?

options.text: The system proposes a plan; an administrator approves it
Only fully automatic and fully manual exist; there is no middle
The middle position is automatic detection with manual data movement
Automatic rebalancing that moves only half of each partition at a time

questions.explanation: Fully automatic systems both decide and move partitions; fully manual systems leave the partition-to-node assignment to an administrator. In between, Couchbase, Riak and Voldemort compute a suggested assignment automatically but require an administrator to commit it before it takes effect.

questions.question: Why is fully automated rebalancing risky?

options.text: Because moving lots of data can overload the network or nodes
Because a partition transfer can corrupt data while it is in flight
Because it requires the database to be taken offline while it runs
Because every partition must be split before it can be moved

questions.explanation: Moving partitions consumes network bandwidth, disk I/O and CPU on both source and destination nodes. Fully automatic movement at the wrong moment can worsen the overload that triggered it.

questions.question: How can automatic rebalancing combined with automatic failure detection make an overloaded node's problem worse?

options.text: A slow node is declared dead, and moving its load adds load to it and the network
A failed node is replaced, and rebalancing completes before clients notice
A network fault splits the cluster into two sides that accept conflicting writes
A full disk triggers rebalancing that frees space on the busy node and its peers

questions.explanation: An overloaded node may be slow to respond, and other nodes can wrongly conclude it is dead. Automatic rebalancing then starts moving its partitions away, which adds transfer load on that same node, on other nodes and on the network, making the overload worse and possibly causing a cascading failure. This is why some systems keep a human in the loop for rebalancing.

questions.question: What is finding the correct current node for a request called?

options.text: Service discovery
Load balancing across the available nodes
Distributed consensus between the nodes
Rebalancing of partitions across nodes

questions.explanation: Partition ownership changes during rebalancing, so a client needs a current IP address and port for the node serving its key. That changing endpoint lookup is the general service-discovery problem.

questions.question: In a partitioned database, which strategies can route a client request to the node owning the right partition?

options.text: Any node forwards; a partition-aware routing tier; or partition-aware clients
Use DNS round-robin only, since DNS records always point at the right partition owner
Broadcast every request to all nodes in the cluster and keep the first reply
Route by hash, by range or at random, without tracking which node owns which partition

questions.explanation: Routing logic may live in a database node, an external partition-aware tier, or the client. Every design still needs a sufficiently current and consistent partition-to-node map after rebalancing.

questions.question: In routing designs that use a coordination service such as ZooKeeper, how do routers learn about partition reassignments?

options.text: Nodes register in ZooKeeper, which keeps the partition map and notifies routers
Routers poll every node on every request to ask which partitions it owns
Nodes gossip the map among themselves and ZooKeeper is read only at startup
ZooKeeper forwards every client request to the owning node on the router's behalf

questions.explanation: All routing participants must agree on which node owns each partition, or requests go to the wrong place. With a coordination service, each node registers in ZooKeeper, ZooKeeper keeps the authoritative partition-to-node mapping, and the routing tier or partition-aware clients subscribe to it. When ownership changes or nodes join or leave, ZooKeeper notifies them. ZooKeeper holds metadata only; it does not carry the request traffic.

questions.question: Which systems track partition assignment with a coordination service such as ZooKeeper, or an equivalent metadata service of their own? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: LinkedIn's Espresso, which uses Helix for cluster management — and Helix in turn relies on ZooKeeper
HBase, SolrCloud and Kafka, which (as of the mid-2010s) used ZooKeeper to track partition assignment
MongoDB, which has a similar architecture but relies on its own config server implementation and mongos daemons as the routing tier
Cassandra and Riak, which both rely on gossip between nodes

questions.explanation: Espresso/Helix, HBase, SolrCloud and Kafka use ZooKeeper-style coordination for partition assignments; MongoDB uses analogous config servers and mongos routers. Cassandra and Riak instead gossip state among database nodes.

optionExplanations.a: Espresso delegates cluster assignment to Helix, and Helix stores and coordinates that state through ZooKeeper.
optionExplanations.b: HBase, SolrCloud and Kafka used ZooKeeper to track membership and partition assignment; Kafka later moved this metadata into its own KRaft quorum.
optionExplanations.c: MongoDB uses config servers as the authoritative metadata store and mongos as the routing tier, which is architecturally similar even without ZooKeeper.
optionExplanations.d: Cassandra and Riak distribute membership and routing knowledge through gossip between database nodes rather than a ZooKeeper-style central coordination service.

questions.question: What routing approach do Cassandra and Riak use?

options.text: Nodes gossip mappings and forward requests
They use a dedicated routing tier, which reduces node complexity but adds a dependency
They require partition-aware clients, which removes all server complexity
They use DNS for routing, which is simple but slow to update

questions.explanation: Cassandra and Riak spread cluster-state changes by gossip, and any node can forward a request to the owner. This removes an external coordinator but moves membership and routing complexity into every node.

questions.question: As of the mid-2010s, how did Couchbase handle routing and rebalancing?

options.text: Couchbase did not rebalance automatically and routed via a tier called moxi
Couchbase relied on ZooKeeper and rebalanced partitions automatically
Couchbase used gossip between nodes and required every client to be partition-aware
Couchbase had no routing layer, so clients always addressed nodes directly

questions.explanation: Couchbase did not rebalance automatically, which simplified its design: partition assignments changed only when an administrator committed a change. Clients were normally routed through a routing tier called moxi, which learned about routing changes from the cluster nodes rather than from ZooKeeper or gossip.

questions.question: How can clients discover router or seed-node addresses?

options.text: Use DNS or a stable seed-node list
Clients must be configured with a static list of every node's IP address
Clients must query ZooKeeper directly to obtain the IP addresses
Clients must broadcast on the local network to discover the nodes

questions.explanation: Router and seed-node addresses change far less often than individual partition assignments. DNS or a configured seed list can therefore bootstrap contact, after which the system supplies current routing metadata.

questions.question: Which query shapes are supported by simple partitioning alone, and how far do most NoSQL distributed datastores go?

options.text: Single-key reads and writes, plus scatter/gather over local indexes
Full SQL with joins and aggregation, which every NoSQL store supports
Only single-key reads and writes, with no scatter/gather capability
Only analytics queries that scan the whole of the dataset

questions.explanation: Simple distributed stores usually handle primary-key operations and sometimes scatter/gather secondary-index queries. Joins, grouping and complex cross-partition plans require a parallel query engine such as those in MPP databases.

questions.question: In a massively parallel processing (MPP) relational database, what does the query optimizer do with a complex warehouse query?

options.text: Splits it into stages and partitions that run in parallel on different nodes
Sends the whole query to the single node that holds the most relevant data
Runs its joins and aggregations one after another on a coordinator node
Rewrites it into many single-key lookups against a distributed key-value store

questions.explanation: MPP means massively parallel processing. Its optimizer turns scans, joins and aggregation into dependent execution stages, partitions each stage's work across nodes, and combines their results.

questions.question: Which queries particularly benefit from parallel execution across partitions?

options.text: Queries that scan large parts of the dataset
Single-key point lookups by primary key
Reads that hit one local secondary index
Writes that update a single small record

questions.explanation: A scan over much of the dataset can divide independent ranges among many nodes and combine their partial results. A single-key lookup already targets one small location, so cross-node parallelism adds overhead rather than useful work.

questions.question: When does partitioning a database become necessary?

options.text: When the data or load is too big for one machine to store or process
Whenever more than one machine is available, to provide fault tolerance
Whenever read latency must be reduced for users in distant regions
Whenever replication fails to keep its copies consistent across the nodes

questions.explanation: Partitioning is justified when one machine cannot store the data or serve the workload. Its benefit depends on both a suitable key-to-partition rule and rebalancing as data, traffic, or cluster membership changes.

questions.question: Describe key range partitioning and its trade-off.

options.text: Sorted keys with one range per partition: good for range scans, risky for hot spots
Keys are hashed and a partition owns a range of hashes; range queries are inefficient
Keys are assigned randomly; there is no hot spot risk
Keys are sorted but partitions are fixed in number and never split

questions.explanation: Each partition owns a contiguous, sorted key range, enabling efficient scans over nearby keys. Uneven or increasing keys can create hot spots, so systems often adjust boundaries by splitting and merging ranges.

questions.question: What is the central trade-off of hash partitioning?

options.text: More even load, at the cost of efficient range queries
Efficient range queries, at the cost of uneven load
Guaranteed even load for every workload, at no cost to range queries
Preserved key order, at the cost of needing a cryptographic hash

questions.explanation: A good hash smooths ordinary key distributions but cannot eliminate application-level hot keys, so evenness is not guaranteed. The cost is that adjacent source keys become unrelated hash values and cannot be scanned together efficiently.

questions.question: Which design combines elements of key-range and hash partitioning?

options.text: Hash one key part to pick the partition; sort by the remaining parts
Combining local and global secondary indexes in one database
Combining a fixed partition count with dynamic partition splitting
Combining replication with partitioning in the same cluster

questions.explanation: A compound key can hash its first component to spread parent entities across partitions, then sort by remaining components inside each partition. This supports local range scans without preserving global key order.

questions.question: Which statements about the two ways of partitioning secondary indexes are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Document-partitioned (local) indexes store the secondary index in the same partition as the primary key and value
With local indexes only a single partition needs to be updated on write, but a read of the secondary index requires a scatter/gather across all partitions
Term-partitioned (global) indexes are partitioned separately by indexed value, so one entry may include records from all primary-key partitions
With global indexes a write touches only one index partition, while a read must scatter/gather across all of them

questions.explanation: Document-partitioned (local) indexes are stored with each partition's own data, so a write touches one partition but a secondary-index read must scatter/gather across all partitions. Term-partitioned (global) indexes are partitioned by indexed value, so one entry can reference records from every data partition; a read goes to one index partition, but one document write may update several. The claim that a global index makes writes single-partition and reads scatter/gather reverses the trade-off.

optionExplanations.a: A document-partitioned index stores each record's secondary entries beside its primary data, so every partition indexes only its local documents.
optionExplanations.b: Local placement makes writes single-partition, but a secondary lookup without the primary partition key must query every partition and combine matches.
optionExplanations.c: A term-partitioned index routes entries by the indexed value, so one term partition can contain references to records from every primary-data partition.
optionExplanations.d: The trade-off is reversed: a global index read can target the term's partition, while one document write may update several independently placed term partitions.

questions.question: Which of these claims about partitioning hold? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Consistent hashing as originally defined works poorly for databases, so hash partitioning is the better term
In fixed-partition rebalancing the assignment of keys to partitions does not change; only the assignment of partitions to nodes does
A term-partitioned index can be partitioned differently from the primary key index
Hashing a key eliminates hot spots entirely, even for a single hot key

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing as Karger et al. defined it works poorly for databases, so 'hash partitioning' is the clearer term. Fixed-partition rebalancing moves whole partitions between nodes without changing which partition a key belongs to. A global (term-partitioned) index is partitioned by indexed value, independently of the primary key. Hashing does not remove every hot spot: all traffic for one identical key still hashes to one partition.

optionExplanations.a: Karger-style consistent hashing has random boundaries and awkward database rebalancing behavior, so hash partitioning is the clearer general term for database designs.
optionExplanations.b: Fixed partitioning keeps the key-to-partition function stable and rebalances by changing only which node owns each complete partition.
optionExplanations.c: A global secondary index routes by indexed terms rather than primary keys, so its partitions can have a completely different layout from the primary data.
optionExplanations.d: All operations for one identical hot key still produce the same hash and reach one partition; hashing spreads distinct keys, not one key's traffic.

questions.question: How are the techniques for routing queries to the right partitions best characterised?

options.text: A spectrum, from partition-aware load balancing to parallel query engines
A binary choice between client-side routing and server-side request routing
A single recommended architecture, built around a ZooKeeper coordination service
A problem with no general techniques, solved afresh by each deployment

questions.explanation: Routing ranges from choosing one node for a simple key lookup, through scatter/gather across several partitions, to an MPP engine coordinating a multi-stage parallel plan. These are degrees of partition awareness, not a binary choice.

questions.question: Which property lets a partitioned database scale, and which problem does it create?

options.text: Partitions operate independently, but cross-partition writes are hard to reason about
Partitions are tightly coupled, which is what makes cross-partition writes easy
Partitions share one global lock, which is what limits scalability
Partitions are replicated, which is what makes cross-partition writes slow

questions.explanation: Each partition operates mostly independently, which is what lets a partitioned database spread across many machines. The price is that an operation writing to several partitions is hard to reason about: if the write to one partition succeeds and another fails, the data is left half-updated. Handling that needs cross-partition atomicity, such as distributed transactions.
